1	# CoralNPU Integration Guide
2	
3	
4	
5	This document describes integrating CoralNPU as an AXI/TileLink peripheral in
6	a bigger system.
7	
8	## AXI
9	
10	We provide a scalar-only CoralNPU configuration that can integrate with an AXI
11	based system. The SystemVerilog can be generated with:
12	
13	``` bash
14	bazel build //hdl/chisel/src/coralnpu:core_mini_axi_cc_library_emit_verilog
15	```
16	
17	### Module interfaces
18	
19	![CoralNPU AXI](images/coralnpu_axi.svg)
20	
21	The interfaces to CoralNPU are defined as follows:
22	
23	|   Signal Bundle  |                   Description                             |
24	| ---------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
25	|       clk        | The clock of the AXI Bus/CoralNPU core.                     |
26	|      reset       | The active-low reset signal for the AXI Bus/CoralNPU core.  |
27	|      s_axi       | An AXI4 slave interface that can be used to write TCMs or touch CoralNPU CSRs. |
28	|      m_axi       | An AXI4 master interface used by CoralNPU to read/write to memories/CSRs. |
29	|       irqn       | Active-low interrupt to the CoralNPU core. Can be triggered by peripherals or other host processor. |
30	|       wfi        | Active-high signal from the CoralNPU core, indicating that the core is waiting for an interrupt. While this is active, CoralNPU is clock-gated. |
31	|      debug       | Debug interface to monitor CoralNPU instructions execution. This interface is typically only used for simulation. |
32	|      halted      | Output interface informing if the Core is running or not. Can be ignored. |
33	|      fault       | Output interface to determine if the Core hit a fault. These signals should be connected to a system control CPU interrupt-line or status register for notification when CoralNPU faults or is halted. |
34	
35	#### AXI master signals
36	
37	AR / AW channel
38	
39	| Signal | Behaviour |
40	| ------ | --------- |
41	| addr   | Address CoralNPU wishes to read/write |
42	| prot   | Always 2 (unprivileged, insecure, data) |
43	| id     | Always 0 |
44	| len    | (Count of beats in the burst) - 1 |
45	| size   | Bytes-per-beat (1, 2, or 4) |
46	| burst  | Always 1 (INCR) |
47	| lock   | Always 0 (normal access) |
48	| cache  | Always 0 (Device non-bufferable) |
49	| qos    | Always 0 |
50	| region | Always 0 |
51	
52	R channel
53	
54	| Signal | Behaviour |
55	| ------ | --------- |
56	| data   | Response data from the slave |
57	| id     | Ignored, but should be 0 as CoralNPU only emits txns with an id of 0 |
58	| resp   | Response code |
59	| last   | Whether the beat is the last in the burst |
60	
61	W channel
62	
63	| Signal | Behaviour |
64	| ------ | --------- |
65	| data   | Data CoralNPU wishes to write |
66	| last   | Whether the beat is the last in the burst |
67	| strb   | Which bytes in the data are valid |
68	
69	B channel
70	
71	| Signal | Behaviour |
72	| ------ | --------- |
73	| id     | Ignored, but should be 0 as CoralNPU only emits txns with an id of 0 (an RTL assertion exists for this) |
74	| resp   | Response code |
75	
76	Note: the USER signal is not supported on any of the channels.
77	
78	#### AXI slave signals
79	
80	AR / AW channel
81	
82	| Signal | Behaviour |
83	| ------ | --------- |
84	| addr   | Address the master wishes to read / write to |
85	| prot   | Ignored |
86	| id     | Transaction ID, should be reflected in the response beats |
87	| len    | (Count of beats in the burst) - 1 |
88	| size   | Bytes-per-beat (1,2,4,8,16) |
89	| burst  | 0, 1, or 2 (FIXED, INCR, WRAP) |
90	| lock   | Ignored |
91	| cache  | Ignored |
92	| qos    | Ignored |
93	| region | Ignored |
94	
95	R channel
96	
97	| Signal | Behaviour |
98	| ------ | --------- |
99	| data   | Response data from CoralNPU |
100	| id     | Transaction ID, should match with the id field from AR |
101	| resp   | Response code (0/OKAY or 2/SLVERR) |
102	| last   | Whether the beat is the last in the burst |
103	
104	W channel
105	
106	| Signal | Behaviour |
107	| ------ | --------- |
108	| data   | Data the master wishes to write to CoralNPU |
109	| last   | Whether the beat is the last in the burst |
110	| strb   | Which bytes in data are valid |
111	
112	B channel
113	
114	| Signal | Behaviour |
115	| ------ | --------- |
116	| id     | Transaction ID, should match with the id field from AW |
117	| resp   | Response code (0/OKAY or 2/SLVERR)
118	
119	Note: the USER signal is not supported on any of the channels.
120	
121	#### Debug Signals
122	
123	| Signal   | Behaviour |
124	| -------- | --------- |
125	| en       | 4-bit value, indicating which fetch lanes are active |
126	| addr     | 32-bit values, containing the PC for each fetch lane |
127	| inst     | 32-bit values, containing the instruction for each fetch lane |
128	| cycles   | cycle counter |
129	| dbus     | Information about internal LSU transactions |
130	| -> valid | Whether the transaction is valid |
131	| -> bits  | addr: The 32-bit address for the transaction |
132	|          | write: If the transaction is a write |
133	|          | wdata: 128-bit write data for the transaction |
134	| dispatch | Information about instructions which are dispatched for execution |
135	| -> fire  | If an instruction was dispatched in the slot, this cycle |
136	| -> addr  | The 32-bit address of the instruction |
137	| -> inst  | The 32-bit value of the instruction |
138	| regfile  | Information about writes to the integer register file |
139	| -> writeAddr | Register addresses to which a future write is expected |
140	| ->-> valid | If an instruction was dispatched in this lane, which will write the regfile |
141	| ->-> bits | The 5-bit register address to which the write is expected |
142	| -> writeData | For each port in the register file, information about writes |
143	| ->-> valid | If a write occurred on this port, this cycle |
144	| ->-> bits_addr | The 5-bit register address to which the write occurred |
145	| ->-> bits_data | The 32-bit value which was written to the register |
146	| float | Information about write to the floating point register file |
147	| -> writeAddr | Register addresses to which a future write is expected |
148	| ->-> valid | If an instruction was dispatched to floating point on this cycle |
149	| ->-> bits | The address of the register to which a write is expected |
150	| -> writeData | For each port in the register file, information about writes |
151	| ->-> valid | If a write occured on this port, this cycle |
152	| ->-> bits_addr | The 5-bit register address to which the writh occurred |
153	| ->-> bits_data | The 32-bit value which was written to the register |
154	
155	
156	### CoralNPU Memory Map
157	
158	Memory accesses to CoralNPU are defined as follows:
159	
160	| Region |      Range        |  Size  | Alignment |                 Description                   |
161	| ------ | ----------------  | ------ | --------- | --------------------------------------------- |
162	|  ITCM  | 0x0000 -  0x1FFF  |   8kB  |  4 bytes  | ITCM storage for code executed by CoralNPU.     |
163	|  DTCM  | 0x10000 - 0x17FFF |  32kB  |  1 byte   | DTCM storage for data used by CoralNPU.         |
164	|  CSR   | 0x30000 - TBD     |   TBD  |  4 bytes  | CSR interface used to query/control CoralNPU.   |
165	
166	### Reset Considerations
167	CoralNPU uses a synchronous reset strategy -- to ensure proper reset behavior, ensure that the clock runs for a cycle with reset active, before enabling either the internal clock gate (via CSR) or gating externally.
168	
169	## Booting CoralNPU
170	A note first -- in these examples, CoralNPU is located in the overall system memory map at 0x70000000.
171	
172	1. The instruction memory of CoralNPU must be initialized.
173	```c
174	volatile uint8_t* coralnpu_itcm = (uint8_t*)0x00000000L;
175	for (int i = 0; i < coralnpu_binary_len; ++i) {
176	    coralnpu_itcm[i] = coralnpu_binary[i];
177	}
178	```
179	
180	If something like a DMA engine is present in your system, that is probably a better option for initializing the ITCM.
181	
182	2. Program the start PC
183	If your program is linked such that the starting address is 0, you may skip this.
184	
185	```c
186	volatile uint32_t* coralnpu_pc_csr = (uint32_t*)0x00030004L;
187	*coralnpu_pc_csr = start_addr;
188	```
189	
190	3. Release clock gate
191	```c
192	volatile uint32_t* coralnpu_reset_csr = (uint32_t*)0x00030000L;
193	*coralnpu_reset_csr = 1;
194	```
195	
196	After this, ensure you wait a cycle to allow CoralNPU's reset to occur.
197	If you want to configure something like an interrupt that is connected to CoralNPU's
198	fault or halted outputs, this is a good time.
199	
200	4. Release reset
201	```c
202	volatile uint32_t* coralnpu_reset_csr = (uint32_t*)0x00030000L;
203	*coralnpu_reset_csr = 0;
204	```
205	
206	At this point, CoralNPU will begin executing at the PC programmed in step 2.
207	
208	5. Monitor for `io_halted`
209	The status of CoralNPU's execution can be checked by reading the status CSR:
210	```c
211	volatile uint32_t* coralnpu_status_csr = (uint32_t*)0x00030008L;
212	uint32_t status = *coralnpu_status_csr;
213	bool halted = status & 1;
214	bool fault = status & 2;
215	```

217	# CoralNPU CSRs
218	Note: These are CSRs that are intended to be read or written externally
219	to CoralNPU, e.g. by the host processor in a system.
220	They are not the same as the RISC-V CSRs accessed via the Zicsr ISA extension.
221	
222	### Register: `RESET_CONTROL`
223	*   **Offset**: `0x0`
224	*   **Description**: Controls reset and clock gating for the CoralNPU core. On power-up, the core is held in reset with its clock gated. To start the core, the clock gate should be released first, followed by de-asserting reset.

230	| 31:2  | `RESERVED`   | Reserved, writes ignored, reads return 0.                                                               | R      | 0           |

237	| :---- | :-------------- | :-------------------------------------------------- | :----- | :---------- |
238	| 31:0  | `START_ADDRESS` | The address where the core will begin execution.    | R/W    | 0           |

3	Coral NPU is a hardware accelerator for ML inferencing. Coral NPU is an Open Source IP designed by Google Research and is freely available for integration into ultra-low-power System-on-Chips (SoCs) targeting wearable devices such as hearables, augmented reality (AR) glasses and smart watches.
4	
5	Coral NPU is a neural processing unit (NPU), also known as an AI accelerator or deep-learning processor. Coral NPU is based on the 32-bit RISC-V Instruction Set Architecture (ISA).
6	
7	Coral NPU includes three distinct processor components that work together: matrix, vector (SIMD), and scalar.
8	
9	![Coral NPU Archicture](doc/images/arch_data_flow.png)

12	## Coral NPU Features
13	Coral NPU offers the following top-level feature set:
14	
15	* RV32IMF_Zve32x RISC-V instruction set (specifically `rv32imf_zve32x_zicsr_zifencei_zbb`)
16	* 32-bit address space for applications and operating system kernels
17	* Four-stage processor, in-order dispatch, out-of-order retire
18	* Four-way scalar, two-way vector dispatch
19	* 128-bit SIMD, 256-bit (future) pipeline
20	* 8 KB ITCM memory (tightly-coupled memory for instructions)
21	* 32 KB DTCM memory (tightly-coupled memory for data)
22	* Both memories are single-cycle-latency SRAM, more efficient than cache memory
23	* AXI4 bus interfaces, functioning as both manager and subordinate, to interact with external memory and allow external CPUs to configure Coral NPU

1	# CoralNPU
2	
3	CoralNPU is a RISCV CPU built with custom SIMD instructions and microarchitectural
4	decisions that align with the dataplane properties of an ML accelerator. The design
5	of CoralNPU starts with domain and matrix capabilities; vector and scalar
6	capabilities are then added for a fused design.
7	
8	## Block Diagram
9	
10	![CoralNPU block diagram](images/coralnpu_block.png)
11	
12	## Scalar Core
13	
14	A simple RISC-V scalar frontend drives the command queues of the ML+SIMD
15	backend.
16	
17	CoralNPU utilizes a custom RISC-V frontend (rv32im) that runs the minimal set of
18	instructions to support an executor run-to-completion model (eg. no OS, no
19	interrupts), with all control tasks onloaded to the SMC . The C extension
20	encoding is reclaimed (as per the risc-v specification) to provide the necessary
21	encoding space for the SIMD registers (6b indices), and to allow flexible type
22	encodings and instruction compression (stripmining) for the SIMD instruction
23	set. The scalar core is an in order machine with no speculation.
24	
25	The branch policy in the fetch stage is backwards branches are taken and forward
26	branches are not-taken, incurring a penalty cycle if the execute result does not
27	match the decision in the fetch unit.
28	
29	Registers        | Names         | Width
30	---------------- | ------------- | -----------------------
31	Scalar (31)      | zero, x1..x31 | 32 bits
32	Control & Status | CSRx          | Various
33	
34	## Vector Core
35	
36	We use SIMD and vector interchangeably, referring to a simple and practical SIMD
37	instruction definition devoid of variable length behaviors. The scalar frontend
38	is decoupled from the backend by a FIFO structure that buffers vector
39	instructions, posting only to the relevant command queues when dependencies are
40	resolved in the vector regfile. The vector core supports data widths of 8, 16, and 32 bits.
41	
42	Registers        | Names         | Width
43	---------------- | ------------- | -----------------------
44	Vector (64)      | v0..v63       | 256 bits (eg. int32 x8)
45	Accumulator      | acc<8><8>     | 8x8x 32 bits
46	
47	
48	### MAC
49	
50	The central component of the design is a quantized outer product
51	multiply-accumulate engine. An outer-product engine provides two-dimensional
52	broadcast structures to maximize the amount of deliverable compute with respect
53	to memory accesses. On one axis is a parallel broadcast (“wide”, convolution
54	weights), and the other axis the transpose shifted inputs of a number of batches
55	(“narrow”, eg. MobileNet XY batching).
56	
57	![CoralNPU MAC](images/coralnpu_aconv.png)
58	
59	The outer-product construction is a vertical arrangement of multiple VDOT
60	opcodes which utilize 4x 8bit multiplies reduced into 32 bit accumulators and
61	performing 256 MACs per cycle.
62	
63	### Stripmining
64	
65	Strip mining is defined as folding array-based parallelism to fit the available
66	hardware parallelism. To reduce frontend instruction dispatch pressure becoming
67	a bottleneck, and to natively support instruction level tiling patterns through
68	the SIMD registers, the instruction encoding shall explicitly include a
69	stripmine mechanism that converts a single frontend dispatch event to the
70	command queue into four serialized issue events into the SIMD units. For
71	instance a “vadd v0” in Dispatch will produce “vadd v0 : vadd v1 : vadd v2 :
72	vadd v3” at Issue. These will be processed as four discrete events.
73	
74	## Cache
75	
76	Caches exists as a single layer between the core and the first level of shared
77	SRAM. The L1 cache and scalar core frontend are an overhead to the rest of the
78	backend compute pipeline and ideally are as small as possible.
79	
80	The L1Icache is 8KB (256b blocks * 256 slots) with 4-way set associativity.
81	
82	The L1Dcache sizing is towards the scalar core requirements to perform loop
83	management and address generation. The L1Dcache is 16KB (SIMD256b) with low set
84	associativity of 4-way. The L1Dcache is implemented with a dual bank
85	architecture where each bank is 8KB (similar to L1Icache). This property allows
86	for a degree of next line prefetch. The L1Dcache also serves as an alignment
87	buffer for the scalar and SIMD instructions to assist development and to
88	simplify software support. In an embedded setting, the L1Dcache provides half of
89	the memory bandwidth to the ML outer-product engine when only a single external
90	memory port is provided. Line and all entry flushing is supported where the core
91	stalls until completion to simplify the contract.
92

1	# Multiplication Unit
2	
3	The Multiply Unit (MLU) executes multiplication operations: MUL, MULH, MULHSU
4	and MULHU.
5	
6	## Interfaces
7	
8	Inputs to the MLU are instructions from the Dispatch Unit or data reads from the
9	Register File. The single MLU in the CoralNPU core can service instructions from
10	any of the four instruction lanes, but only one command is dispatched in any
11	cycle.
12	
13	Outputs of the MLU are writes to the Register file.
14	
15	Figure 1 shows the inputs and outputs to and from the MLU.
16	
17	![image](../images/mlu_interfaces.png)
18	
19	Figure 1: Mlu interfaces
20	
21	### MLU Inputs
22	
23	Note: There are 4 instances of each of these signals (one for each instruction
24	lane).
25	
26	| Signal Name  | Type          | Description                                                        |
27	| ------------ | ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
28	| req.valid    | Bool          | If the command if valid.                                           |
29	| req.op       |               | The function to execute.                                           |
30	| req.addr     | UInt(5)       | The RegFile address to write the result to.                        |
31	| req.ready    | Bool (output) | If the command is accepted. Used in a ready-valid hand-shake.      |
32	| rs1.valid    | Bool          | If there is a valid rs1 read this cycle. Only used for assertions. |
33	| rs1.data     | UInt(32)      | The rs1 data read from the RegFile.                                |
34	| rs2.valid    | Bool          | If there is a valid rs1 read this cycle. Only used for assertions. |
35	| rs2.data     | UInt(32)      | The rs2 data read from the RegFile.                                |
36	
37	### MLU Outputs
38	
39	| Signal Name | Type     | Description                                                                       |
40	| ----------- | -------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
41	| rd.valid    | Bool     | If the command if valid.                                                          |
42	| rd.addr     | UInt(5)  | The RegFile address to write the result to.                                       |
43	| rd.data     | UInt(32) | The computation result to write to RegFile.                                       |
44	| rd.ready    | Bool     | If the write result is accepted by the RegFile. Used in a ready-valid hand-shake. |
45	
46	### Timing/Pipeline
47	
48	The MLU is a three stage pipeline, with the following stages:
49	
50	1. **Dispatch:** The dispatch unit determines if MLU operations can be executed.
51	Amongst the four lanes, the MLU accepts the first valid MLU instruction. This
52	request will be processed next cycle.
53	2. **Compute:** The second stage performs computation of the multiplication,
54	using the register read data from rs1 and rs2.
55	2. **Writeback:** The multiplication result is stored back to the register file.

1	# CoralNPU Microarchitecture
2	
3	![image](../images/microarch.png)
4	
5	## Pipeline
6	
7	The CoralNPU base processor is an in-order three-stage pipeline capable of
8	dispatching up to 4 instructions per cycle. The instruction stages are:
9	
10	* **Instruction fetch:** Instructions are fetched from memory into an
11	instruction buffer.
12	* **Decode/Dispatch:** The first 4 instructions in the instruction buffer are
13	decoded. Interlock and scoreboard logic determine which of the instructions can
14	be dispatched this cycle. Instructions are forwarded to their respective
15	execution units.
16	* **Execute/Writeback:** Execution units with dispatched instructions read
17	operands from the register file and perform computation. Results can also be
18	written back to the register file in the same cycle.
19	
20	Some execution units can take multiple cycles to execute. Instruction latencies
21	can be found in the table below:
22	
23	| Instruction Type | Latency (cycles) | Description            |
24	| ---------------- | ---------------- | ---------------------- |
25	| Alu              | 1                | Add, sub, xor, ...     |
26	| Csr              | 1                | CSR instructions       |
27	| Bru              | 1                | bge, jal, ebreak, ...  |
28	| Mlu              | 2                | mul, mulh, ...         |
29	| Dvu              | Variable         | div, rem, ...          |
30	| Lsu              | 2+               | lw, sw, ...            |
31

1	# Load Store Unit
2	
3	![image](../images/lsu.svg)
4	
5	The Load Store Unit handles memory operations issued by the core. Functionally,
6	it's purpose is to translate memory instructions into transactions on the
7	appropriate subsystem.
8	
9	## Slots
10	
11	The CoralNPU LSU uses a concept called _slots_ to handle memory transactions. A
12	slot is a data structure which manages the state of a single dispatched LSU
13	operation and determines what memory transaction should be performed. At its
14	core, there exists a table in each slot which tracks which part of the memory
15	operation has been completed.
16	
17	For example, below is the slot table for a word-store into address 0xDEADBEEF:
18	
19	| Index | Active |   Address  | Data |
20	| ----- | ------ | ---------- | ---- |
21	|   0   |    1   | 0xDEADBEEF | 0x01 |
22	|   1   |    1   | 0xDEADBEF0 | 0x23 |
23	|   2   |    1   | 0xDEADBEF1 | 0x45 |
24	|   3   |    1   | 0xDEADBEF2 | 0x67 |
25	|   4   |    0   | 0xDEADBEF3 | 0x00 |
26	...
27	|   n   |    0   | 0xDEADBEF3 | 0x00 |
28	
29	Memory transactions over TCM or AXI busses will read/write data in the slot
30	table and flip the active bits to 0 as they are made.
31	
32	The typical lifetime of a slot is as follows:
33	
34	1) **Idle**: An idle slot will dequeue a LsuOperation from the command queue.
35	Scalar operations will move directly into **Transfer Memory** while vector
36	operations will go to the **Vector Update** state.
37	2) **Vector Update**: For vector operations masks, addresses (for indexed ops)
38	and data (for store ops) need to be received from the RvvCore. This stage is
39	bypassed for scalar operations.
40	3) **Transfer Memory**: While there are still active entries in the slot table,
41	the active entry with the lowest "index" will be selected for a memory
42	transaction. A scatter/gather unit will then select all other active entries
43	(although not necessarily contiguous) that will be bundled with the transaction.
44	The appropriate memory bus (ibus, dbus, ebus) will then be selected and a memory
45	transaction will be conducted. When there are no active entries, the slot moves
46	into the next state (**Writeback**).
47	4) **Writeback**: Once all memory transactions are completed, the result must
48	be written back to register files. Additionally, vector stores are
49	"acknowledged" back to the RvvCore. Scalar and floating point scores bypass this
50	stage. Once writeback is completed, the slot moves back into the
51	**Vector Update** state for LMUL > 1, or the **Idle** state.
52	
53	CoralNPU currently uses one "slot" in the LSU. In the future, multiple slots maybe
54	added to allow multiple operations to partake in the same transaction.
55	
56	## Interfaces
57	
58	### LSU Command Interface
59	
60	The LSU has a command interface coming from the dispatch unit and register file.
61	
62	| Signal Name   | Type          | Description                                                   |
63	| ------------- | ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
64	| req.valid     | Bool          | If the LSU command is valid.                                  |
65	| req.op        |               | The LSU operation to execute.                                 |
66	| req.addr      | UInt(5)       | The RegFile address to write the result to for loads.         |
67	| req.pc        | UInt(32)      | The PC of the LSU instruction. Use for fault reporting.       |
68	| req.elemWidth | UInt(32)      | Used in the RVV only. The EEW for strided loads.              |
69	| req.ready     | Bool (output) | If the command is accepted. Used in a ready-valid hand-shake. |
70	
71	### Bus Interfaces
72	
73	| Signal Name | Type              | Description                                                       |
74	| ----------- | ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
75	| ibus.valid  | Bool              | If the ibus transaction is valid.                                 |
76	| ibus.addr   | UInt(32)          | The address of the ibus transaction.                              |
77	| ibus.rdata  | UInt(128) (input) | The data read from the ibus. Arrives one cycle after hand-shake.  |
78	| ibus.ready  | Bool (input)      | If the transaction is accepted. Used in a ready-valid hand-shake. |
79	
80	| Signal Name | Type              | Description                                                       |
81	| ----------- | ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
82	| dbus.valid  | Bool              | If the dbus transaction is valid.                                 |
83	| dbus.addr   | UInt(32)          | The address of the dbus transaction.                              |
84	| dbus.size   | UInt(5)           | The size of this transaction in bytes.                            |
85	| dbus.pc     | UInt(32)          | The PC of the LSU instruction. Use for fault reporting.           |
86	| dbus.rdata  | UInt(128) (input) | The data read from the dbus. Arrives one cycle after hand-shake.  |
87	| dbus.wdata  | UInt(128)         | The data to write from the dbus.                                  |
88	| dbus.wmask  | UInt(16)          | A byte write mask for this transaction.                           |
89	| dbus.ready  | Bool (input)      | If the transaction is accepted. Used in a ready-valid hand-shake. |
90	
91	| Signal Name      | Type              | Description                                                       |
92	| ---------------- | ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
93	| ebus.valid       | Bool              | If the ebus transaction is valid.                                 |
94	| ebus.addr        | UInt(32)          | The address of the ebus transaction.                              |
95	| ebus.size        | UInt(5)           | The size of this transaction in bytes.                            |
96	| ebus.pc          | UInt(32)          | The PC of the LSU instruction. Use for fault reporting.           |
97	| ebus.rdata       | UInt(128) (input) | The data read from the ebus. Arrives one cycle after hand-shake.  |
98	| ebus.wdata       | UInt(128)         | The data to write from the ebus.                                  |
99	| ebus.wmask       | UInt(16)          | A byte write mask for this transaction.                           |
100	| ebus.ready       | Bool (input)      | If the transaction is accepted. Used in a ready-valid hand-shake. |
101	| ebus.fault.valid | Bool (input)      | Raised if a fault occurs on the external bus.                     |
102	| ebus.fault.write | Bool (input)      | If the fault occured on a write operation.                        |
103	| ebus.fault.addr  | Bool (input)      | The address of the memory transaction when the fault occurred.    |
104	| ebus.fault.epc   | Bool (input)      | The PC of the instruction that triggered the fault.               |
105	| ebus.internal    | Bool              | Not used.                                                         |
106	
107	### Writeback Interfaces
108	
109	| Signal Name | Type     | Description                                              |
110	| ----------- | -------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
111	| rd.valid    | Bool     | If the writeback to the scalar regfile is valid.         |
112	| rd.addr     | UInt(5)  | The address of the scalar register file to writeback to. |
113	| rd.data     | UInt(32) | The data to write to the scalar register file.           |
114	
115	| Signal Name     | Type     | Description                                                      |
116	| --------------- | -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
117	| rd_flt.valid    | Bool     | If the writeback to the floating point regfile is valid.         |
118	| rd_flt.addr     | UInt(5)  | The address of the floating point register file to writeback to. |
119	| rd_flt.data     | UInt(32) | The data to write to the floating point register file.           |
120	
121	### RVV Interfaces
122	
123	For the RVVCore, the LSU contains the following interfaces:
124	
125	| Signal Name            | Type              | Description                                                       |
126	| ---------------------- | ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
127	| rvv2lsu.valid          | Bool              | If the rvv2lsu transaction is valid.                              |
128	| rvv2lsu.idx.valid      | Bool              | If there is valid index data from the vector register file.       |

1	# Debug Module
2	
3	## Overview
4	
5	The debug module implements a subset of the RISC-V Debug Specification, providing external debug support for the CoralNPU core. It allows a debugger to halt, resume, and single-step the core, as well as read and write core registers and memory.
6	
7	## Architecture
8	
9	The debug module is a standalone module that connects to the core via a dedicated debug interface. It communicates with an external debugger through a simple request/response protocol.
10	
11	The following diagram illustrates the high-level architecture of the debug module:
12	
13	![Debug Module Architecture](debug_arch.png)
14	
15	## Interfaces
16	
17	The following table describes the internal hardware interfaces of the debug module:
18	
19	| Name           | Direction | Type                  | Width | Description                               |
20	|----------------|-----------|-----------------------|-------|-------------------------------------------|
21	| **ext.req**    | Input     | Decoupled             |       | External debugger request.                |
22	| ↳ `valid`      |           | Bool                  | 1     | The request is valid.                     |
23	| ↳ `ready`      |           | Bool                  | 1     | The module is ready for a request.        |
24	| ↳ `bits`       |           | DebugModuleReqIO      |       | The request payload.                      |
25	|   ↳ `address`  |           | UInt                  | 32    | The address of the register to access.    |
26	|   ↳ `data`     |           | UInt                  | 32    | The data to write.                        |
27	|   ↳ `op`       |           | DmReqOp               | 2     | The operation to perform (NOP, READ, WRITE).|
28	| **ext.rsp**    | Output    | Decoupled             |       | External debugger response.               |
29	| ↳ `valid`      |           | Bool                  | 1     | The response is valid.                    |
30	| ↳ `ready`      |           | Bool                  | 1     | The debugger is ready for a response.     |
31	| ↳ `bits`       |           | DebugModuleRspIO      |       | The response payload.                     |
32	|   ↳ `data`     |           | UInt                  | 32    | The data read from the register.          |
33	|   ↳ `op`       |           | DmRspOp               | 2     | The result of the operation (SUCCESS, FAILED, BUSY).|

60	| havereset      | Input     | Bool                  | 1     | Core has been reset.                      |
61	
62	## Command Protocol
63	
64	An external debugger communicates with the debug module by reading and writing a set of memory-mapped Control and Status Registers (CSRs) over the AXI interface. These CSRs provide a communication channel to the debug module's internal registers.
65	
66	### Write Operation
67	
68	To write to an internal debug module register (e.g., writing `0x1` to `dmcontrol` at address `0x10`):
69	
70	1.  **Poll for readiness:** Read the `status` CSR at `0x31014` and wait for bit 0 to be `1`.
71	2.  **Set address:** Write the target internal register address (`0x10`) to the `req_addr` CSR at `0x31000`.
72	3.  **Set data:** Write the data (`0x1`) to the `req_data` CSR at `0x31004`.
73	4.  **Initiate write:** Write the `WRITE` operation code (`2`) to the `req_op` CSR at `0x31008`.
74	5.  **Poll for response:** Read the `status` CSR at `0x31014` and wait for bit 1 to be `1`.
75	6.  **Check status:** Read the `rsp_op` CSR at `0x31010` to confirm the operation was successful.
76	7.  **Acknowledge response:** Write to the `status` CSR at `0x31014` to clear the response.
77	
78	### Read Operation
79	
80	To read from an internal debug module register (e.g., reading from `dmstatus` at address `0x11`):
81	
82	1.  **Poll for readiness:** Read the `status` CSR at `0x31014` and wait for bit 0 to be `1`.
83	2.  **Set address:** Write the target internal register address (`0x11`) to the `req_addr` CSR at `0x31000`.
84	3.  **Initiate read:** Write the `READ` operation code (`1`) to the `req_op` CSR at `0x31008`.
85	4.  **Poll for response:** Read the `status` CSR at `0x31014` and wait for bit 1 to be `1`.
86	5.  **Check status:** Read the `rsp_op` CSR at `0x31010` to confirm the operation was successful.
87	6.  **Read data:** Read the result from the `rsp_data` CSR at `0x3100c`.
88	7.  **Acknowledge response:** Write to the `status` CSR at `0x31014` to clear the response.
89	
90	## AXI CSR Interface
91	
92	These registers are mapped into the CoralNPU CSR address space and are used to communicate with the debug module.
93	
94	| Address    | Name       | Description                                                                                                |
95	|------------|------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
96	| 0x30800    | req_addr   | Write the target debug module register address here.                                                       |
97	| 0x30804    | req_data   | Write data for the debug module operation here.                                                            |
98	| 0x30808    | req_op     | Write the operation type (e.g., READ, WRITE) to this register to initiate a debug module command.          |
99	| 0x3080c    | rsp_data   | After a command completes, the data result is available here.                                              |
100	| 0x30810    | rsp_op     | After a command completes, the status result (e.g., SUCCESS, FAILED) is available here.                    |
101	| 0x30814    | status     | A read-only register to check the status of the debug module. Bit 0 indicates if the module is ready for a new request. Bit 1 indicates if a response is available. |
102	
103	## Internal Debug Module Registers
104	
105	The debug module implements a set of internal registers that are accessible to an external debugger via the AXI CSR interface. These registers are used to control and monitor the core.
106	
107	| Address | Name         | Description                               |
108	|---------|--------------|-------------------------------------------|
109	| 0x04    | data0        | Data register for abstract commands.      |
110	| 0x10    | dmcontrol    | Debug module control register.            |
111	| 0x11    | dmstatus     | Debug module status register.             |
112	| 0x12    | hartinfo     | Hart information register.                |
113	| 0x16    | abstractcs   | Abstract command status register.         |
114	| 0x17    | command      | Abstract command register.                |
115	
116	### dmcontrol (0x10)
117	
118	The `dmcontrol` register is used to control the debug module and the core.
119	
120	| Bits  | Name      | Description                                                                 |
121	|-------|-----------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
122	| 31    | haltreq   | Request to halt the core.                                                   |
123	| 30    | resumereq | Request to resume the core.                                                 |
124	| 29:2  | reserved  | Reserved for future use.                                                    |
125	| 1     | ndmreset  | Reset the debug module.                                                     |
126	| 0     | dmactive  | Activate the debug module.                                                  |
127	
128	### dmstatus (0x11)
129	
130	The `dmstatus` register provides the status of the debug module and the core.
131	
132	| Bits  | Name       | Description                                                                 |
133	|-------|------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
134	| 11    | allrunning | All harts are running.                                                      |
135	| 10    | anyrunning | Any hart is running.                                                        |
136	| 9     | allhalted  | All harts are halted.                                                       |
137	| 8     | anyhalted  | Any hart is halted.                                                         |
138	| 7:4   | reserved   | Reserved for future use.                                                    |
139	| 3:0   | version    | Debug module version.                                                       |
140	
141	### abstractcs (0x16)
142	
143	The `abstractcs` register provides the status of abstract commands.
144	
145	| Bits  | Name     | Description                                                                 |
